lectures.name: Diagnosis in Psychiatry
lectures.title: Diagnosis in psychiatry
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ There is no lesion, test or scan in psychiatry: the diagnosis is made by matching the interview to operational criteria (symptoms, number, duration, exclusions, specifiers). Clinically significant distress or impairment is required for almost every diagnosis. An expected response to loss or stress is not a disorder. Other specified gives the reason criteria are not met; unspecified does not. The five axes were abandoned in DSM-5; the biopsychosocial formulation answers "why this person, today?"

Psychiatry has no lesion to find, so how do you make a diagnosis that holds up? You match what the interview gives you against operational criteria (the DSM-5), then put the person back around the checklist with a formulation.
1. Why psychiatric diagnosis is different

• Psychiatry = the biopsychosocial study of disorders of cognition, perception, emotion and behaviour
  • Unlike neurology, there is no identifiable lesion: no physical sign, blood test, biopsy or scan makes the diagnosis
    • the diagnosis rests on the clinical interview and observation
    • a diagnosis names a cluster of symptoms and signs thought to share a pathological process
  • A good diagnosis is valid (accurate) and reliable (stable)
    • validity, three kinds: conceptual (the criteria pick out the right people) · construct (separates conditions with different causes) · predictive (patients follow the same course over time)
    • the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5) exists to make diagnoses more valid and reliable
  • Almost every diagnosis requires clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other functioning
2. What a diagnosis is not

• An expected or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss
  • Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) or a conflict between the person and society, unless it comes from a dysfunction in the person
3. Types of psychiatric disorder, by what is impaired

rows: Dementia · psychotic disorders · major depression and bipolar disorder · obsessive-compulsive disorder · anxiety · dissociative disorders · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
Conduct disorder · oppositional defiant disorder · anxiety · personality disorders · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder

blocks.html: 4. Using the DSM-5: operational criteria

• Operational criteria = a set of conditions the patient must meet to receive the diagnosis; they improve reliability
  • Match the interview against each part:
    • key symptoms · threshold number of symptoms · duration · key exclusions (better explained by a substance, a medical condition or another disorder) · specifiers (severity, remission, features, subtypes)
  • Pitfalls
    • normal reactions to stress are not accounted for → false positives
    • symptoms too mild to be a disorder
    • symptoms over-endorsed or fabricated · symptoms fluctuate and depend on the patient's account
    • "check-the-box" interviewing that loses the patient's narrative (not patient-centred)
5. Putting the person back in: formulations
• Multi-axial formulation - dropped as a formal structure in DSM-5, still a useful reference:

rows: Clinical disorders (major mental disorders, learning disorders)
Personality disorders and intellectual disability (lifelong, shape Axis I)
Acute medical conditions and physical disorders
Level of functioning (clinical judgement, severity measures)

blocks.html: • Biopsychosocial formulation - the more holistic picture DSM-5 favours: answers "why this person, with this presentation, on this day?"
6. False negatives, and when criteria are not met

• False negatives happen even with a standard approach
    • patients minimize symptoms or present atypically → handled by interviewing skill
    • real dysfunction, but full criteria are not met
  • When criteria are not met:
    • Other specified = you state the reason the criteria are not met
    • Unspecified = no reason given (e.g. not enough information, as in the emergency room)

lectures.name: The Psychiatric Interview
lectures.title: The psychiatric interview
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Balance content (information, symptoms) with process (rapport, empathy) - without the relationship the patient will not share the content. The history of presenting illness takes at least half the interview, funnels open → closed, and needs a reference point ("When were you last well?"). Screen safety every time, including thoughts of harming others. The mental status exam is gathered during the interview, not after it. Ask about diabetes and lipids in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The interview is the psychiatric investigation: it has to gather the content (information, symptoms) while building the process (rapport, empathy) that lets the patient share it. The sections below follow the order of the interview.
1. Two components, held in balance

rows: The therapeutic relationship that makes the patient trust you with sensitive information

blocks.html: 2. Introduction and identification

• Introduce yourself and your role · put the patient at ease · show respect and interest · attend to comfort
  • Identifying data: name · gender (ask pronouns if not obvious) · age ("what is your age?") · marital status · parental status (who is caring for the children now?) · occupation and finances · cultural background
3. History of presenting illness

• At least half the interview
  • Funnel strategy: open-ended questions first ("What brought you in today?") → closed, verifying questions ("Do you isolate yourself when depressed?")
  • Reference point - define what "present" means: "When were you last well?" · "When were you content with how you were functioning?"
    • separates the present episode from the past psychiatric history
  • Precipitants: relationship difficulties · stopping treatment or a medication change · substance use · medical illness or new medical drugs
4. Psychiatric screening (before the past history)

rows: Down or less interested most of the day, nearly every day, for 2 weeks or more → then sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, guilt, slowing or restlessness, suicide
A period "up", "high" or persistently irritable, not when intoxicated → grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, risky pleasure-seeking
Sudden rush of symptoms peaking within 10 minutes, some out of the blue, then 1 month or more of fear of another attack or changed behaviour
Avoiding places in case of an attack · fear of being unable to escape or get help
Fear of a specific thing (heights, blood, flying) causing avoidance, distress or interference
Intrusive thoughts, images or urges that keep coming back · driven, repeated actions (washing, checking, counting)
Excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday things with physical effects
A very upsetting event → nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance, gaps in memory, loss of enjoyment
Fear of being watched, the focus of attention, or humiliated, with avoidance
Beliefs others find odd · being spied on, mind read, thoughts inserted, special messages · voices or visions · only when sad, high or irritable?
Use despite harm, danger or legal trouble · 3+ drinks in 3 hours on 3+ occasions · tolerance · failed attempts to stop · withdrawal · over 2 hours a day spent on it

blocks.html:
• Safety - always: thoughts of killing yourself or not waking up · self-harm · thoughts of hurting others · unsafe driving · unprotected sex · arrests
    • older adults: the 3 F's - fire, flood, falls
5. Past psychiatric history

• Goals: the longitudinal course · severity · predisposing, precipitating and protective factors
  • The illness: age of onset · first symptoms and triggers · functioning before and after · number and length of hospitalizations
  • Its impact: "How is your life different?" · "How do you cope?" · "What opportunities were lost?"
  • Treatments: biological (medications - names, doses, durations) · physical (electroconvulsive therapy, transcranial magnetic stimulation, bright light) · psychosocial (cognitive behavioral therapy, skills training) · "Has anything made a difference?"
6. Mental status exam
• Gathered mostly by observation during the interview, not as a separate step - components by ABC STAMP LICKER
7. Medical history, chosen by disorder

rows: Weight loss (melancholic depression) · obesity (carbohydrate craving in seasonal depression)
Skin lesions (crystal methamphetamine) · abscesses · HIV, hepatitis B and C (injection drug use) · alcoholic pancreatitis
Skin picking, excoriation, maceration from handwashing

blocks.html: 8. Family and personal history

• Family history - in biological relatives: mental illness · alcohol or drugs · eccentric behaviour · suicide attempts or deaths · estrangement
    • non-biological relatives still matter (an alcoholic step-parent shapes the environment, not the genes)
  • Personal history - go chronologically from childhood, once rapport exists, with the hypothesis in mind
    • development (pregnancy and birth briefly, home situation, attachment, clear rules) · childhood adversity (violence, punishment out of proportion, sexual abuse) · school · childhood personality · relationships and supports · sexual history · legal history · occupational history
9. Ending the interview and the plan

• Don't finish on a sensitive topic · thank the patient · acknowledge their commitment · ask what you missed and how they feel now · discuss the plan
  • Treatment plan: most urgent next steps · safety issues · inpatient or outpatient · treatment approach · psychological supports

lectures.name: Phenomenology and the Mental Status Exam
lectures.title: Phenomenology and the mental status exam
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Affect is what you observe in the moment; mood is what the patient reports over time - and you comment on whether they are congruent. Circumstantial gets to the point; tangential never does. Flight of ideas → mania; loosening of associations → psychosis. Hallucination = no stimulus; illusion = real stimulus misread. Ego-syntonic suicidal thoughts are the higher-risk kind. The mental status exam is gathered during the interview, in every encounter.

Phenomenology asks how the patient experiences a symptom, not just which symptom it is; the mental status exam (MSE) is the objective record of what you observed. The exam is the "physical exam" of psychiatry, laid out by ABC STAMP LICKER.
1. Phenomenology

• Two meanings:
    • Phenomenological psychopathology = objective description of the signs and symptoms (the "what")
    • Karl Jaspers = empathic, neutral description of the subjective experience - the one the lecture focuses on, as part of the art of medicine
  • The skill: elicit the symptom and understand how the patient lives it
    • "auditory hallucinations" does not tell you what it is like to hear voices
    • physicians treat "who's", not "what's"
2. The mental status exam: what it is

• The objective part of the assessment · the "physical exam" of psychiatry
  • Not a separate part of the interview - assessed on the fly as you talk · is a separate heading in a case presentation
  • Done in every encounter, in every field, not only with mental illness
3. The components: ABC STAMP LICKER

rows: Grooming, dress for the setting and weather, oddities, tattoos, track marks
Calm or restless, slowed, pacing · abnormal movements (tremor, tics)
Willing, guarded, evasive, argumentative, over-familiar, eye contact · accessibility (willing and able to share?)

Rate, rhythm, tone, volume, latency, articulation, amount · errors: mutism, fast speech (tachylalia), cluttering, repeating own words (palilalia), apraxia, dysarthria · pressured speech points to a thought disorder
Form (process) - how it flows (§4) · Content - delusions, obsessions, preoccupations, safety
Observed, in the moment: dysphoric, euthymic, euphoric, irritable, labile · range (restricted, blunted, flat) · appropriate to content? congruent with stated mood?
Patient's own description, over time ("1 to 10, 5 is your normal")
Insight = understands the illness and what drives it · judgement = appreciates the consequences of choices
Orientation, attention, memory, executive function, abstraction · not formally tested unless there is a concern (then the Mini-Mental State Examination or Montreal Cognitive Assessment)
Knowledge = what you know · intelligence = what you do with it
Consistent with other data and within the interview? gaps? logical history?

blocks.html:
• Judgement sits under Insight in the upper-year notes and under Knowledge base in the vault note (sources differ - check the slides)
  • A poor choice is not a mental illness: people have the right to make unwise decisions
4. Thought form: getting from A to B

rows: Detours through irrelevant detail, but gets to B
Rapid jumps from tangent to tangent, links barely visible
No logical connection between thoughts - the most severe

blocks.html:
• Derailing: the upper-year notes treat it as the same as loosening of associations; the vault note lists it separately as abruptly losing the train of thought (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Also: illogical, perseverative
5. Thought content and perception

• Delusion = a fixed, false belief out of keeping with the patient's cultural norms
    • themes: persecutory, grandiose, jealousy, somatic, erotomanic, nihilistic, religious, control, reference
    • bizarre (impossible) vs non-bizarre (possible) · mood-congruent, incongruent or neutral
    • overvalued ideas also go here (e.g. misreading things as being about you)
  • Perception:

rows: Any sense; auditory commonest (commanding vs commenting); not always pathological
Experienced through an "inner sense", not truly through the senses

blocks.html: 6. Endings: safety

• Suicidal thoughts: passive (thinking about it) vs active (planning or acting) · self-injury
    • ego-syntonic (not distressing to the patient) = higher risk - a red flag · ego-dystonic = distressing
  • Homicidal thoughts: assessed the same way

lectures.name: Organ Donation
lectures.title: Organ donation
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The family can refuse donation in both opt-in and opt-out systems, even when the patient registered. Neurologic death = no consciousness + no brainstem reflexes + apnea, whole brain, known cause, no confounders. Circulatory death = arterial pressure under 5 mmHg, then 5 minutes hands-off, declared by 2 physicians. Nova Scotia is Canada's only opt-out province. Organs need donation close to death; tissue can wait - and every death is referred for tissue. Normothermic regional perfusion grew the donor pool by 30-50%.

Organs must be taken very close to the time of death; tissues can be taken after it. The lecture turns on the two routes to deceased organ donation - death by neurologic criteria and death by circulatory criteria - and on what makes families say yes.
1. The Canadian framework

rows: Sharing organs across provincial borders (equitable access) · monitoring performance · national policies and guidelines · national campaigns · legal and ethical challenges
Provincial organizations (Ontario: Trillium Gift of Life Network)
Their own policies and regulations within the national framework · choosing opt-in or opt-out

blocks.html: • Trillium: patient-facing, 24/7, coordinates sharing across Canada and the United States
2. Opt-in vs opt-out consent

• Opt-out (presumed) consent - aims to close the gap between supply and demand
    • used in many countries, including Spain (the world's highest donor rate)
    • Nova Scotia, 2021 - the only Canadian province; all others are opt-in
    • families of all medically suitable donors are approached · donors rose afterwards (other changes may have contributed)
  • In both models, the family can still refuse - even if the patient registered as a donor · rare, because most families follow the patient's wishes
3. Pathways to donation

• The brain dies when starved of oxygen, three ways: ① injury and swelling cut off its blood flow · ② the heart stops · ③ breathing stops
  • Refer to Trillium when a GIFT trigger is present:
    • Grave prognosis (Glasgow Coma Scale under 3, as written in the note - check the threshold on the slides) · Injured brain with no recovery expected · Family raises donation · Therapy being limited

blocks.html: 4. Death by neurologic vs circulatory criteria

rows: Decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment · medical assistance in dying (MAiD) · unsuccessful resuscitation
Complete absence of consciousness + absent brainstem reflexes

Known cause · no confounding factors · absent brainstem reflexes · absent breathing effort on the apnea test · whole-brain (not just brainstem) death · absent cerebral blood flow (blood-flow test or cerebral angiogram)

Withdrawal as usual · continuous arterial line · pressure under 5 mmHg · 5 minutes hands-off (no return of circulation, so death is permanent) · 2 physicians declare death (time of death = end of the 5 minutes)

blocks.html: 5. Optimizing the donor and the organs

• What is good for the patient is good for the organs: blood pressure with fluids and pressors · lung protection (steroids) · nutrition · hormone replacement (e.g. levothyroxine) · hypothermia for kidney donors
  • Circulatory-death donors: direct procurement perfusion · machine perfusion · normothermic regional perfusion - new, ↑ the donor pool by 30-50% and improves transplant volume and outcomes
  • Tissue donation: every patient who dies is referred; if suitable, the family is approached
6. What makes families say yes

• Families may refuse because of:
    • perceived quality of care (a gap in their loved one's care)
    • not understanding brain death
    • timing - feeling rushed, asked straight after the prognosis talk
    • setting - asked somewhere public rather than a private room
    • not enough information, or an untrained approach
  • Building the relationship
    • communication: right place · often · clear language · several formats
    • trust: emotional support · physical needs · dignity and respect · enough information
    • time: to talk with staff, to decide, to be with their loved one
  • Culture and faith: many faiths actively support donation as a good deed at the end of life · faith leaders want to help explain their faith's position to their communities

lectures.name: Depressive Disorders
lectures.title: Depressive disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Major depression = 5 of 9 symptoms for 2 weeks, one of them low mood or anhedonia, and never a manic or hypomanic episode. Persistent depressive disorder = the rule of 2's: 2 years, 2 symptoms, never 2 months well. DMDD: outbursts 3 times a week for 12 months, onset before 10, diagnosed only from 6 to 18. Atypical = mood reactivity, hypersomnia, weight gain, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity; melancholic = no reactivity, worse mornings, early waking. SSRIs first line, 4-6 weeks to respond; ECT first line when treatment is urgent or there are psychotic or catatonic features - 80-90% response. Light therapy first line for seasonal depression. No antidepressants in bipolar disorder.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Every depressive disorder shares sad, empty or irritable mood with somatic and cognitive changes that impair function; they are told apart by symptom count, duration, age, timing and cause. Then: why depression happens (biological, psychological, social) and how it is treated.
1. The depressive disorders

• Major depressive disorder (MDD) · persistent depressive disorder (PDD, dysthymia) · disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) · premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) · substance-induced depressive disorder · depressive disorder due to another medical condition · other specified and unspecified
  • An expected, culturally approved response to a stressor or loss is not a disorder
2. Major depressive disorder

• The commonest depressive disorder · single episode or recurrent (2 or more)
    • recurrence risk climbs: 50-60% after the first episode · 75% after the second · 90% after the third
  • A major depressive episode = criteria A-C
    • A: 5 or more of 9 symptoms, in the same 2 weeks, a change from before - at least 1 must be depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia) (mnemonic SIGECAPS)
      • depressed mood · loss of interest or pleasure · weight or appetite change (more than 5% of body weight in a month) · insomnia or hypersomnia · psychomotor agitation or slowing (seen by others) · fatigue · worthlessness or excessive guilt · poor concentration or indecision · recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
      • "nearly every day", most of the day
    • B: clinically significant distress or impairment
    • C: not due to a substance or another medical condition
  • D: not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder
  • E: never a manic or hypomanic episode (otherwise it is bipolar)
3. Specifiers (what kind of episode)
• Severity (mild · moderate · severe) · remission (full = no significant symptoms for 2 months) · early or late onset

rows: 2 or more: keyed up · restless · can't concentrate from worry · dread · fear of losing control
3 or more manic symptoms during the depression (elevated mood, grandiosity, pressured talk, racing thoughts, more energy, risky activity, less need for sleep)
Seen by others · a risk factor for bipolar disorder, not mania itself
1: pleasure lost or no mood reactivity + 3: despair/emptiness · worse in the morning · early morning waking · agitation or slowing · weight loss · guilt
Mood reactivity + 2 or more: weight gain · hypersomnia · leaden paralysis · rejection sensitivity
3 or more of 12 (stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia)
Onset in pregnancy or up to 4 weeks after delivery
~3% in pregnancy, 6% after · may be psychotic (infanticide risk) · recurrence 30-50%
2 major depressive episodes in 2 years tied to a time of year, with remission at a set time
MDD only · hypersomnia, overeating, carbohydrate craving · higher latitude, younger age

blocks.html: 4. Telling the depressive disorders apart

rows: 5 of 9, including low mood or anhedonia
Low mood most days + 2 of 6 (appetite, sleep, energy, self-esteem, concentration, hopelessness)
2 years (1 year in children, mood may be irritable) · never symptom-free over 2 months - the rule of 2's
Milder but longer · MDD criteria may be met throughout ("double depression") · never cyclothymic
Temper outbursts 3 or more times a week + irritable mood between
12 months, in 2 of 3 settings · onset before 10 · first diagnosed only between 6 and 18
Never a full manic or hypomanic episode over 1 day
5 symptoms in the week before menses, at least 1 mood symptom (lability, irritability, low mood, anxiety)
Most cycles · improves within days of menses · confirmed by daily ratings over 2 cycles
Not just a flare of another disorder
During or soon after intoxication, withdrawal or a medication
The substance can cause it · not only during delirium
Direct physiological result of the illness on history, exam or labs · not adjustment disorder with depressed mood (where the illness is the stressor) · not only during delirium
Recurrent brief (2-13 days, monthly for 12 months) · short-duration (4-13 days) · insufficient symptoms (2 weeks, fewer symptoms)
Full criteria not met - reason not stated
e.g. emergency room, not enough information

blocks.html: 5. Why depression happens

• Multifactorial and heterogeneous: genes × environment · early (childhood) onset = more psychosocial · later onset = more genetic
  • Genetics: twin concordance 40-50% · first-degree relatives 2-3× · many small-effect genes, serotonin system best studied (e.g. the serotonin transporter) · a family history is not required
    • more heritable: onset before 30 · high recurrence · psychosis · comorbid anxiety or alcohol use
  • Brain: cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, reward centres and hypothalamus all involved · neurotrophic hypothesis = atrophy (neuron and glial loss, thinner cortex)
  • Hormones: ↑ cortisol in 50% (overactive stress axis) · blunted thyrotropin (TSH) response to thyrotropin-releasing hormone · ↓ growth hormone in sleep
  • Sleep: often the presenting symptom · rapid eye movement (REM) sleep comes sooner (↓ REM latency) and there is more of it

rows: Strongest link - depletion → depression and suicide · why selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and tricyclic antidepressants work
↓ = amotivation, fatigue, fog (Parkinson's, reserpine) · ↑ improves mood (bupropion, stimulants) · excess in mania
↑ acetylcholine may cause depression · low GABA → anxiety, agitation · glutamate drives inflammation
↓ by stress, restored by long-term antidepressants

blocks.alt: norepinephrine serotonin dopamine symptom overlap - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: What each monoamine is thought to drive: norepinephrine alertness and energy, serotonin impulsivity and obsessions, dopamine drive and reward; all three overlap at mood and cognition

blocks.html: • Psychological: poor attachment in the first 18 months, loss, anger turned inward · learned helplessness · cognitive triad - negative views of self, world and future

blocks.cap: The cognitive triad: negative automatic thoughts about the self, the world and the future

blocks.html: • Social: stress often precedes the first episode · loss of a parent before age 11 · stress-diathesis model = a pre-existing vulnerability activated by life stress
6. Approach to a depressed patient
7. Treatment

• Choosing an antidepressant: STEPS (safety, tolerability, effectiveness, price, simplicity) · before starting: history, exam, liver tests, blood count, creatinine · weigh other medications (interactions), suicidal ideation, other psychiatric illness (no antidepressants in bipolar disorder), the depression subtype
    • suicide risk can rise early in treatment: energy returns before mood, giving the energy to act
  • Rules: SSRIs first line for most · 4-6 weeks to respond · vegetative symptoms improve first, cognitive later · best = medication + psychotherapy + social support
    • first episode: 6-12 months of medication · 2 or more episodes: 2-5 years or lifelong
  • Not working: ↑ dose → add a second antidepressant of another class (e.g. bupropion) or augment (lithium, thyroid hormone, stimulants, buspirone, atypical antipsychotics) → switch, preferably to another class
  • After remission: stay on it 6 months or more (up to a year in the upper-year notes; longer if recurrent or severe) · watch for recurrence · taper slowly - over 3-6 weeks in the vault note, 1-3 weeks in the upper-year notes (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT): fastest and most effective - 80-90% response · not a last resort
    • first line: urgent need (starving, acutely suicidal) · psychotic or catatonic features · previous good response
    • also mania, catatonic schizophrenia, Parkinson's, refractory epilepsy, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and more
    • relative contraindications only: raised intracranial pressure · recent brain bleed · recent heart attack · brain tumour · berry aneurysm · pheochromocytoma
    • preparation: hold psychotropics (especially benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants, z-drugs) · fasting · glucose check · general anaesthetic without intubation · seizure 20-60 seconds
  • Light therapy: first line for seasonal pattern · 10,000 lux each morning, 45-60 minutes, started before the usual month of onset · also bipolar and non-seasonal depression · as effective as fluoxetine
  • Psychotherapy: cognitive behavioural therapy and interpersonal therapy first line · stress reduction · social interventions (peer support, psychoeducation, community links)

lectures.name: Pharmacology of Antidepressants
lectures.title: Pharmacology of antidepressants
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ SSRIs are first line because they are safe in overdose and well tolerated - never combine them with an MAOI (2-week washout, longer after fluoxetine). Fluoxetine: longest half-life, no discontinuation syndrome, least weight gain, most activating. Paroxetine: sedating, anticholinergic, discontinuation syndrome. Sertraline: diarrhea. Citalopram: avoid with QT or heart problems. Venlafaxine raises diastolic pressure; duloxetine helps neuropathic pain. Bupropion: no sexual effects or weight gain, but lowers the seizure threshold - avoid in eating disorders and brain injury. Mirtazapine: sleep and weight gain. TCAs: cardiac toxicity is the most serious effect. MAOIs + tyramine = hypertensive crisis. Serotonin syndrome = clonus and hyperreflexia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome = rigidity with reduced reflexes.

Every antidepressant raises monoamines in the synapse; the classes differ in which ones, and in their side effects and interactions. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line because they are the safest; the older classes are limited by toxicity and interactions.
1. The classes at a glance

rows: Block serotonin reuptake → more serotonin at the postsynaptic neuron
Most prescribed for major depression · response close to 70%
Sexual (25-50%) · gastrointestinal (GI) · insomnia or sedation · headache · tremor · mania induction
Never with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) or L-tryptophan (2-week washout, longer for fluoxetine) · interactions · liver disease
Depression and anxiety · efficacy and tolerability better than SSRIs
↑ diastolic blood pressure · nausea · sexual · discontinuation syndrome
Augmenting agent · second line for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
No weight gain, sexual effects or sedation · can cause anxiety, insomnia · psychosis at high doses
↑ seizure risk (450 mg+) · avoid in brain injury and eating disorders · does not treat anxiety · abuse potential
Weight gain · very sedating · ↑ cholesterol and triglycerides
Secondary (safer): nortriptyline, desipramine · tertiary: amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine
Non-selective serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake block, plus many receptors
Anticholinergic · antihistamine · orthostatic hypotension · cardiac toxicity (the most serious) · sexual
Amoxapine: depression with anxiety or agitation
Block breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine
Usually third line: no response or intolerance · past good response · atypical depression
Tyramine → hypertensive crisis · serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs · not in children

blocks.html: 2. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors

• Safer than TCAs (far less risk of a fatal overdose) · starting dose ≈ therapeutic dose · better adherence
  • Only fluoxetine has pregnancy-safety evidence (upper-year notes)

rows: Short half-life, no active metabolite · sedating - give at night for anxiety or insomnia
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor · most anticholinergic · weight gain · constipation · discontinuation syndrome
GI effects, especially diarrhea · absorbed best on a full stomach
Longest half-life - no discontinuation syndrome, missed doses matter less · activating · least weight gain
Builds up (avoid in liver disease) · many interactions · activation → anxiety, insomnia, mania
Sedating · GI · avoid with heart disease: slow heart rate, long QT, low potassium or magnesium, recent heart attack, decompensated heart failure

blocks.cap: How an SSRI works: blocking the serotonin reuptake transporter leaves more serotonin in the synaptic cleft for the postsynaptic receptor

blocks.html:
• Side effects by system: sexual 25-50% (delayed orgasm, ↓ libido, ↓ arousal) · GI (nausea 11-16%, diarrhea with sertraline, constipation with paroxetine, appetite loss with fluoxetine) · central nervous system (jitteriness, insomnia with fluoxetine, sedation with paroxetine and fluvoxamine, headache, tremor, mania)
    • the Introduction to Psychopharmacology note gives sexual dysfunction 50-80% (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Interactions: fluvoxamine is a strong CYP450 inhibitor · paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6, lasting up to 5 weeks after stopping · choose the drug least likely to interact (e.g. citalopram)
3. Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors

rows: Almost no CYP450 interactions · short half-life, fast renal clearance
Dose-dependent ↑ diastolic pressure (10-15 mmHg) · nausea · discontinuation syndrome · QT prolongation · sexual (over 30%)
Active metabolite of venlafaxine · hot flashes in menopause
Helps physical symptoms and neuropathic pain · less blood pressure rise
CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 inhibitor · capsule must not be broken

blocks.html: 4. Tricyclics and monoamine oxidase inhibitors

• TCA side effects, by receptor blocked
    • muscarinic → dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dilated pupils, urinary retention
    • histamine → drowsiness, weight gain
    • alpha-1 adrenergic → orthostatic hypotension
    • ↑ norepinephrine in the heart → palpitations, fast heart rate - the most serious
  • TCA interactions: levels ↑ by cimetidine, SSRIs, antipsychotics · ↓ by smoking and lithium · additive sedation with alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids
  • MAOIs: type A breaks down serotonin and norepinephrine; type B trace amines; both break down dopamine
    • tyramine foods (aged cheese, beer, red wine, cured and pickled foods) → hypertensive crisis
    • no serotonergic co-drugs: meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs, sumatriptan, linezolid, cold remedies

blocks.cap: Non-selective MAOIs (isocarboxazid, phenelzine, tranylcypromine) block MAO-A and B and raise serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine; selective MAO-B inhibitors raise dopamine and are used in Parkinson's disease

blocks.html: 5. Serotonin syndrome and discontinuation syndrome

• Serotonin syndrome - toxic, potentially life-threatening excess serotonin
    • causes: therapeutic dose, overdose, or combinations (SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + TCA) · illicit drugs (ecstasy, cocaine, amphetamines, LSD)
    • presents as: hyperreflexia and clonus · tremor · hyperthermia · agitation, confusion · sweating, fast heart rate, dilated pupils, diarrhea
    • differential: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (slow onset, reduced reflexes, rigid in all limbs, very high creatine kinase) · anticholinergic toxicity · meningitis
    • treatment: stop the drug · supportive care · sedatives (benzodiazepines) · serotonin antagonist (cyproheptadine)

blocks.cap: Hunter criteria: on a serotonergic drug plus spontaneous clonus, inducible or ocular clonus with agitation, sweating or high tone and fever, or tremor with hyperreflexia

blocks.html:
• Discontinuation syndrome - after stopping or cutting a drug taken for at least a month
    • dizziness · anxiety · mood swings · insomnia · nausea, usually within 3 days
    • worst with short half-lives (paroxetine, venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine) · not with fluoxetine
    • prevent it: psychoeducation at the first prescription and a slow taper

lectures.name: Introduction to Psychopharmacology
lectures.title: Introduction to psychopharmacology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Typical antipsychotics block D2 everywhere (→ parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia); atypicals block D2 mainly in the mesolimbic pathway plus serotonin 5-HT2 (→ metabolic syndrome, weight gain). Clozapine: agranulocytosis and the most weight gain. Risperidone: high prolactin. Antipsychotic symptoms improve in order: agitation → psychosis → negative symptoms; non-adherence is the #1 cause of relapse. Lithium: tremor, hypothyroidism, diabetes insipidus; not in kidney failure; Ebstein's anomaly in pregnancy. Benzodiazepines: wide safety margin but dependence; delirium in the elderly. Stimulants: avoid with tics.

Psychotropic drugs act on the central nervous system by changing one step of neurotransmission at the synapse. The lecture tours the five families - antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers, benzodiazepines and stimulants - by indication and side effect.
1. Psychotropics and their targets

• Psychotropic = a drug acting on the central nervous system (sleep, wakefulness, sedation, hallucinations) that can cause dependence when misused · controlled by law (Controlled Drugs and Substances Act)
  • Neuroplasticity = the nervous system reorganizing its structure and connections; synaptic plasticity changes the strength of transmission - underlies learning, memory and recovery
  • Drugs can act at any step: synthesis · storage · metabolism · release · reuptake · degradation · the receptor · signalling inside the cell

blocks.alt: pharmacological targets at the synapse - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The ten places a drug can act at a synapse, from the presynaptic action potential through synthesis, storage, release and reuptake to the postsynaptic receptor

rows: GABA-A modulators: benzodiazepines (sedative), barbiturates (anaesthetic) · GABA-B agonist baclofen (muscle relaxant) · valproate, tiagabine (seizures) · too much → coma
Targets in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
D2 antagonists = antipsychotics · D2 agonists for Parkinson's and high prolactin · reuptake inhibitors for depression, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, smoking cessation
Mood, sleep, appetite, sex, anger, gut

Reuptake inhibitors (selective serotonin, serotonin-norepinephrine, tricyclic) · monoamine oxidase inhibitors · receptor agonists (migraine, anxiety) · antagonists (antipsychotics, antiemetics) · mirtazapine
Reuptake inhibitors (tricyclic, serotonin-norepinephrine) · monoamine oxidase inhibitors · stimulants for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder

blocks.html: 2. The families at a glance

rows: D2 block mostly in the mesolimbic pathway + serotonin 5-HT2 block
Psychosis (positive and negative symptoms) · bipolar · add-on in depression
Extrapyramidal (parkinsonism) from nigrostriatal block · tardive dyskinesia · high prolactin
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) · serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs: venlafaxine, duloxetine) · bupropion · mirtazapine
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction (commonest) · gastrointestinal (GI) upset · serotonin syndrome
Lithium · valproate · carbamazepine · lamotrigine · atypical antipsychotics
Sedation · amnesia · delirium in the elderly · dependence, tolerance · respiratory depression

blocks.html: 3. Antipsychotics

blocks.cap: Antipsychotics sit on the postsynaptic D2 receptor and block dopamine released from the presynaptic terminal

blocks.html:
• Indications
    • primary psychosis: schizophrenia · bipolar disorder · severe major depression
    • secondary psychosis: dementia · substance use
    • movement disorders: Tourette syndrome · Huntington's disease
    • others: severe anxiety · aggression · some personality disorders · nausea and vomiting
  • Principles: "start low and go slow" · judge effect at 4-6 weeks · treat 3-6 months past resolution, then ↓ dose 20% every 6 months if stable
    • improvement order: ① anxiety, agitation, insomnia → ② delusions and hallucinations → ③ negative symptoms
    • schizophrenia duration: first episode 2-3 years · recurrent 5 years · 3 or more episodes lifelong
    • non-adherence is the #1 cause of relapse in schizophrenia

rows: Anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, confusion; worse in the elderly)
Weight gain (40% of patients → diabetes, hypertension, high lipids)

blocks.html: • Pregnancy: avoid in the first trimester if possible
4. Antidepressants

• SSRIs: block serotonin reuptake → more serotonin in the cleft · changing one monoamine shifts the others
    • ✔ fewer side effects than tricyclics · safe with heart conduction disease and epilepsy · ✘ not more effective than tricyclics · sexual dysfunction 50-80% · GI upset · serotonin syndrome
    • effect takes 3-4 weeks here, 4-6 weeks in the antidepressant lectures; sexual side effects 50-80% here, 25-50% in the antidepressant lecture (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Others: SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine) · bupropion · mirtazapine
  • Antipsychotic add-ons in severe depression: aripiprazole and brexpiprazole are first-line adjuncts
5. Mood stabilizers: lithium

• Indications: bipolar disorder (treat and prevent) · severe cyclothymia · schizoaffective disorder · recurrent or antidepressant-resistant depression · aggression in schizophrenia
  • Side effects by system: neurologic - tremor (treat with propranolol), cognitive slowing · endocrine - goiter, hypothyroidism · cardiac - benign T-wave changes, sinus node dysfunction · renal - diabetes insipidus (mostly reversible) · skin - acne, hair loss · GI - nausea, vomiting, diarrhea · weight gain
  • Contraindications
    • kidney failure - cleared by the kidney, competes with sodium for reabsorption in the proximal tubule
    • pregnancy - teratogenic in the first trimester: Ebstein's anomaly (heart malformation)
  • Other mood stabilizers: anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, topiramate, gabapentin) · atypical antipsychotics · benzodiazepines · verapamil · clonidine · levothyroxine
6. Benzodiazepines and sleeping pills

• ✔ wide therapeutic index, low toxicity, few interactions · ✘ dependence and tolerance
  • Side effects: drowsiness, dizziness · poor concentration · confusion and delirium (elderly, brain lesions) · paradoxical aggression · anterograde amnesia (worst with lorazepam, triazolam) · teratogenic · respiratory depression (especially by injection)
  • Sleeping pills: hypnotic benzodiazepines (flurazepam, temazepam) - long half-life, morning "hangover"
    • Z-drugs: half-life 6 hours or less → less hangover
7. Stimulants

• Methylphenidate (and pemoline) for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder - can cause tics; avoid with a personal or family history of tics
  • Amphetamines: high abuse risk, can cause hallucinations, delusions, agitation
  • Modafinil (norepinephrine reuptake block) for narcolepsy

lectures.name: Suicide
lectures.title: Suicide
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mental illness is the strongest predictor, but the red flags - active threats, seeking means, hopelessness - mark imminent risk. Egosyntonic, active ideation with a detailed plan and access to means is the highest-risk picture. Previous attempts are a huge risk factor - map the chain of events. Safety contracts are not acceptable; a patient-driven safety plan is. Admit only for acute stabilization; long admissions harm the chronically suicidal. Older men have the highest rate; women self-harm more.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

A suicide risk assessment weighs three things against each other: risk factors (who is vulnerable over a lifetime), warning signs (what is pushing them now) and protective factors (what holds them back). The disposition - admit or manage as an outpatient - follows from acuity, severity, risk and the patient's safety net.
1. Epidemiology

• Not rare: about 12% report suicidal ideation at some point
  • Over 90% of people who die by suicide had a mental health condition - but suicide also happens with no known mental illness
  • Highest-risk group: older men · men use more lethal means and are ~3× more likely to die · women self-harm more
  • Indigenous (First Nations) rates are much higher - about 3×, 9× in youth (upper-year notes)
  • 9th leading cause of death overall · 2nd at ages 10-29 (upper-year notes)
2. Principles of the assessment

• The therapeutic relationship is step #1: unhurried, empathic, honest listening · validate and thank them for sharing · non-judgemental · a private setting
  • Communication: clear language · reframe a question rather than let it be dodged
  • Collateral history supports or challenges the story · privacy and culture can limit it · involve the circle of care for continuity
  • Document (medicolegal and continuity) in a Suicide Risk Assessment: level of risk with the rationale · history · recent changes · previous attempts · risk factors, warning signs, protective factors
  • Culture: both the patient's and the physician's (stigma, taboo) · individualize the plan
3. Risk factors, warning signs, protective factors

rows: Raise lifetime risk · persistent · some unchangeable (male sex)
Promote or start suicidal behaviour now - imminent risk
Lower risk, build resilience · usable in the plan

Mental illness - the strongest predictor, especially schizophrenia, personality disorders (borderline), major depression · physical illness: severe chronic non-cancer pain, chronic disease (Parkinson's disease) · psychosocial: guilt, shame, isolation, poor supports, poor coping, big life changes
"IS PATH WARM": Ideation · Substance use · Purposelessness · Anger · Trapped · Hopelessness · Withdrawal (social, not from drugs) · Anxiety · Recklessness · Mood changes
Strong relationships · belonging · self-esteem · future orientation (goals) · clinical support and willingness to use it

blocks.html:
• Red flags (highest-risk warning signs): active threats · talking about wanting to die · seeking access to means · hopelessness
  • Protective factors lose their weight when risk is severe
4. What the patient presents with

• Non-suicidal self-injury: not a cry for help - it serves a purpose · explore the motivation
  • Ideation - two axes:

rows: No effort to consider, plan or act · may be intrusive and unwanted
Effort to consider, plan, move to action
Clashes with identity and values · distressing, unwanted
Fits current ideals · not distressing - red flag, high risk

blocks.html:
• Plans: get a detailed description (never assume you have enough) · access to means
  • Previous attempts - a huge risk factor: number (include this one) · method and intent · circumstances · how they survived · response to surviving · the chain of events leading up (where to intervene)
    • an "impulsive" attempt may be a long-held plan suddenly activated - ask
  • Underlying themes: control (of one's fate, or of others) · avoidance (escape from pain, money, legal problems, illness) · unbearable distress (abandonment, bereavement, chronic pain)
5. Disposition and management

blocks.html:
• Treating the underlying cause is the most important step (psychiatric or not) - it also prevents future risk
  • Chronic ideation: hospital only for acute stabilization · long admissions build reliance on external control · explore the motives behind any self-harm
6. Neurobiology

• Heritable apart from mental illness: family studies · monozygotic > dizygotic twin concordance · adoptees resemble biological, not adoptive, relatives · no single "suicide gene"
  • Epigenetics: life experience (trauma) alters gene expression (DNA methylation, histone modification, microRNA)
  • Stress axis: hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity - the basis of the stress-diathesis model
  • Serotonin: ↓ serotonin metabolite (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) in cerebrospinal fluid · imaging: ↑ serotonin receptor expression but ↓ binding in the prefrontal cortex · ↓ serotonin transporter binding
  • Also: norepinephrine dysfunction · low serum cholesterol (may act through serotonin)

blocks.cap: Stress-diathesis model: the disorder appears once stress exceeds the threshold set by predisposition

lectures.name: Bipolar Disorders
lectures.title: Bipolar disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Bipolar I needs only one manic episode (≥ 1 week, or any length if hospitalized, or with psychosis); bipolar II needs hypomania (≥ 4 days, no psychosis, no admission) plus a major depression. Cyclothymia: 2 years of subthreshold highs and lows, never well over 2 months. Never an antidepressant alone in bipolar I depression - stop antidepressants and stimulants in mania. Lithium: kidneys, thyroid, parathyroid, Ebstein's. Lamotrigine: rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, slow titration. Valproate: neural tube defects. Clozapine and carbamazepine: agranulocytosis. Major depression is the commonest misdiagnosis.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The bipolar disorders are sorted by how high the mood goes: full mania (bipolar I), hypomania with major depression (bipolar II), or neither reaching threshold for 2 years (cyclothymia). Treatment rests on mood stabilizers - and never on an antidepressant alone.
1. Epidemiology and course

• Lifetime prevalence (Canada): bipolar I disorder 0.87% · bipolar II disorder 0.67% (a 9-country study gives 0.6% and 0.4%)
  • Onset: average 25 years, in three groups - early ~17 (~42%) · middle ~24 (~25%) · late ~32 (~34%) · ⅓ to ⅔ have their first episode in childhood or adolescence
    • earlier onset → longer delay to treatment, more depression, anxiety and substance use
  • Sex: women - more bipolar II, rapid cycling, seasonal pattern, longer depressions, episodes clustered in the reproductive years · men - more bipolar I, more substance use, more completed suicide
  • Progressive course: each episode → ↑ recurrence, ↑ length and severity of later episodes, ↓ threshold for the next, ↑ dementia risk
  • Morbidity: euthymic ~half the time · ill time is mostly depression (~70% in bipolar I, ~82% in bipolar II)
  • Comorbidity is the rule: substance use 33-45% · anxiety 24-56% · personality disorders ~42% · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) 10-20% · treat the bipolar disorder first, then the comorbidity once mood is stable
  • Stigma (public and self-stigma) delays and erodes treatment
2. The episodes

• Manic episode
    • A: abnormally, persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood + increased energy or activity, most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 1 week (any duration if hospitalized)
    • B: 3 or more (4 if the mood is only irritable) - mnemonic DIGFAST: Distractibility · Indiscretion (spending, sex, investments) · Grandiosity · Flight of ideas or racing thoughts · Activity ↑ or agitation · Sleep need ↓ (rested after 3 hours) · Talkative, pressured speech
    • C: marked impairment, or hospitalization, or psychotic features
    • D: not a substance or medical condition
  • Hypomanic episode: the same symptoms for at least 4 days · an unequivocal change observable by others · not severe enough for marked impairment or hospitalization · psychosis makes it mania by definition
  • An episode that starts on an antidepressant (or ECT) but persists beyond the drug's effect counts → bipolar diagnosis

rows: A change in function, but not marked

blocks.html: 3. Telling the bipolar disorders apart

rows: Many hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms, neither reaching an episode
≥ 2 years (1 in youth) · symptomatic ≥ half the time · never well > 2 months

blocks.html: • Specifiers include rapid cycling (≥ 4 episodes in 12 months), mixed features, psychotic features, peripartum onset, seasonal pattern

blocks.cap: Mood over time in unipolar depression, bipolar I, bipolar II and cyclothymia

blocks.html: 4. Diagnosis and differential

• Diagnosis often takes up to 10 years · major depressive disorder is the most frequent misdiagnosis (patients present depressed and don't recall or recognise hypomania)
  • Psychotic disorders are the first diagnosis in 30% - psychosis without mood symptoms points there
  • Others: borderline (true euphoria and long well intervals are extremely rare) · narcissistic (grandiosity without mood change) · antisocial · substance or medication (stimulants, steroids, L-dopa, antidepressants) · medical (brain injury, frontal tumours, multiple sclerosis, stroke, Cushing's, hyperthyroidism)
  • Children: mania overlaps with ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) - in mania the change is episodic and mood-related, with ↓ need for sleep and no daytime sleepiness · older adults: depressive and cognitive symptoms dominate
  • Workup: family history · collateral · prospective mood charting · Mood Disorders Questionnaire screens, does not diagnose · suicide risk assessment at every visit
5. Treatment

blocks.html:
• Psychosocial (adjunct): psychoeducation - the only first-line psychosocial treatment in maintenance (spot prodromes, stress, adherence, stigma) · cognitive behavioural therapy and family-focused therapy for acute depression and relapse prevention · interpersonal and social rhythm therapy for relapse prevention (little acute evidence)
  • Choosing a drug: prior response · safety and tolerability · predominant polarity · prognostic features · discuss with patient and supports
  • Antidepressants: second-line adjuncts only · avoid with past antidepressant-induced mania, mixed features or recent rapid cycling · never monotherapy in bipolar I depression
    • the In-Class note names only quetiapine, cariprazine and lurasidone as approved for bipolar depression, while the guideline figure lists lithium and lamotrigine first line and cariprazine second (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT): second line · refractory illness or need for speed (imminent suicide, catatonia, psychotic depression, medical instability)
  • Light therapy: helps acute bipolar depression · does not cause switching · no evidence for remission
  • Supplements: omega-3, N-acetylcysteine promising but conflicting
  • Before starting: medical history · BMI · pregnancy test and contraception · HLA-B test before carbamazepine

• Weight gain: high - atypicals, clozapine, valproate, lithium, gabapentin · low - lamotrigine, carbamazepine, ziprasidone

  • All three classes (anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antipsychotics) ↑ fracture risk · pregnancy choices: 12 - Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages

lectures.name: Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders
lectures.title: Psychotherapies in mood and anxiety disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ CBT targets thoughts and behaviour with structured sessions and homework; IPT targets current relationships through one of four focus areas and never addresses transference; psychodynamic therapy interprets transference and the unconscious; DBT was built for borderline personality disorder. Supportive therapy bolsters defences; psychodynamic therapy challenges them. CBT and IPT are first line for major depression. Psychotherapy matches medication for many disorders and its effects last longer. Suitability needs motivation, psychological mindedness and ego strength - not psychosis.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Each evidence-based therapy is defined by what it targets - the unconscious past (psychodynamic), thoughts and behaviours (CBT), current relationships (IPT) or emotional dysregulation (DBT) - and that target decides which patient it suits. Most work about as well as medication, and their effects last longer.
1. What psychotherapy is, and who it suits

• Treatment of mental illness with psychological interventions - usually talking, plus the therapeutic relationship and tailored strategies
  • Evidence-based: psychodynamic · cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) · interpersonal therapy (IPT) · dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) · family · group
    • effectiveness similar to medication, sometimes better (DBT beats any drug for borderline personality disorder) · effects outlast medication
  • Common factors behind much of the benefit: accurate empathy · unconditional positive regard · genuineness · a strong working relationship · professionalism · goal-directed problem-solving
  • Suitable patients: significant suffering · strong motivation · psychological mindedness (thinks abstractly about problems, capable of insight into their own role) · ego strength (intact reality testing - not psychotic, frustration tolerance, impulse control) · can form relationships (keeps a job, has relationships outside therapy)
2. The therapies compared

rows: The unconscious shapes patterns (psychic determinism) · make the unconscious conscious
Bolster defences to help the person function
Schemas → automatic thoughts → cognitive distortions drive feelings and behaviour
Symptoms are a response to current relationship problems · medical "sick role"
Emotional dysregulation + an invalidating environment → extreme behaviours (self-harm) to cope
Interpretation · confrontation · clarification · transference · defences · working through
Praise · reassurance · reframing · advice · anticipatory guidance
Socratic questioning · thought records · behavioural activation · behavioural experiments
Skills groups · chain analysis · validation · dialectics · phone coaching
Not (yet) suitable for other therapy · adjustment disorder
Major depression (first line) · anxiety (exposure) · bipolar depression and relapse
Developed for depression - first line · peripartum depression (role change)

blocks.html: 3. Psychodynamic (insight-oriented) therapy

• Freud's structure: id (unconscious drives) · superego (conscience, internalized rules) · ego (conscious self, balances reality against both)
  • Process: free association → the therapist links past and present and finds recurring patterns · goal: change dysfunctional interpersonal patterns · the relationship is a "corrective emotional experience"
    • techniques: observation (outside awareness) · confrontation (aware but avoided) · clarification · encouragement to elaborate · empathic validation · psychoeducation · advice and praise
  • Transference: the patient casts the neutral ("blank screen") therapist in a role from their past · countertransference: the clinician's own reaction to the patient
  • Object relations: past relationships re-enacted in the present
  • Defence mechanisms reduce signal anxiety, can become pathological: displacement (emotion moved to another object) · reaction formation (into its opposite) · isolation of affect (idea split from feeling) · projection (own impulses attributed to others)
  • Working through: repeated observing, clarifying, confronting and interpreting until the patient takes responsibility for their patterns
  • Supportive therapy sits at the supportive end of this continuum: it bolsters defences where psychodynamic therapy challenges them
4. Cognitive behavioural therapy
• Beck, originally for major depression · thoughts, emotions and behaviours feed each other

blocks.cap: The CBT cycle: thoughts create feelings, feelings create behaviour, behaviour reinforces thoughts

blocks.html:
• Session structure: greet → symptom check → set agenda → review homework → work on the agenda → teach the cognitive model → set new homework → summarize and get feedback
  • Socratic questioning ("what is the evidence?") challenges cognitive distortions (cognitive restructuring): all-or-nothing · selective abstraction · personalization · magnification · minimization · arbitrary inference · overgeneralization
  • Downward arrow questioning reaches the core belief ("she doesn't like me" → "no one likes me" → "I am a loser")
  • Thought record: situation · thought · emotion · behaviour
  • Behavioural activation: act before you feel better · activity scheduling rated for accomplishment and pleasure
  • Behavioural experiments: test a belief · in anxiety, exposure

blocks.cap: Beck's cognitive triad: negative views of the self, the world and the future

blocks.html: 5. Interpersonal therapy

• Built from research on the psychosocial side of depression · shorter, present-focused, structured alternative to psychodynamic therapy
  • Choose one focus: role disputes · role transitions · grief (a real death) · interpersonal deficits
  • Interpersonal inventory at the start (relationships changing around symptom onset) · treatment contract · each session opens with the week ("how have things been?") and links symptoms to life events
  • Problem-solving: accept the situation, negotiate for change, or leave
6. Dialectical behaviour therapy

• Made specifically for borderline personality disorder · behavioural strategies + Buddhist-derived mindfulness and acceptance
  • Assumptions: patients are doing their best and need to change · they may not have caused their problems but must solve them
  • Modes: individual therapy (1-1.5 hours a week) · group skills (mindfulness, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, distress tolerance) · telephone coaching (ideally 24/7) · therapist consultation team
  • Patient agreement: attend, reduce suicidal behaviour, cut therapy-interfering behaviour, attend groups - break it and therapy ends
  • Stages: ① severe behavioural dyscontrol (stop life-threatening behaviour) → ② quiet desperation (trauma symptoms, dissociation) → ③ problems in living → ④ incompleteness (contentment, connection)
  • Wise mind = middle ground between reasonable and emotional mind · chain analysis of antecedents → behaviour → consequences · remove reinforcers of self-harm · validation
7. In practice

• Mostly delivered by allied health (psychologists, social workers) · often eclectic · principles still useful to every physician · mind boundaries
  • Access: insurance (community psychologist, social worker) · low-cost community agencies · outpatient psychiatry referral for severe illness (hospital group therapy) · some psychiatrists and family physicians bill provincial insurance (OHIP)

lectures.name: Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses
lectures.title: Depression and anxiety in medical illness
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, anhedonia and suicidal ideation are not normal in medical illness - they point to depression. Stroke carries the highest depression rate (22-50%). Adjustment disorder → supportive therapy; major depression → antidepressants; hypoactive delirium → treat the cause. Start low, go slow, but reach a therapeutic dose. Cardiac: sertraline first line; tricyclics and MAOIs contraindicated. Diabetes: SSRIs or SNRIs; tricyclics worsen glucose control.

Depression in the medically ill is common, treatable, and missed because of myths - the discriminating question is whether the psychological symptoms (hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt, anhedonia, suicidal thoughts) are present, because illness alone does not cause them. Neither source covers anxiety in medical illness separately (check the slides).
1. Epidemiology

• Rates rise with the type, number and acuity of illnesses · in older patients, 3 comorbid illnesses = 3× suicide risk, 5 = 5×
  • Bidirectional: major depression is a risk factor for diabetes, heart disease, stroke, hypertension, obesity, cancer and dementia
  • Major depression raises mortality 60-80%, with or without chronic illness
2. Why it happens

• Disease factors: neurotransmitter changes · chronic pain · anxiety about recovery
  • Psychosocial: grief for the pre-illness self · disability · trauma · isolation · money, housing, food
  • Chronic stress: poor nutrition, low income, substance use · a sustained stress response → hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity → immune activation (pro-inflammatory cytokines), sympathetic activation, corticotropin-releasing factor pathways
  • Cytokine-induced "sickness behaviour" mimics depression: weakness · poor concentration · malaise · hypersomnia · anorexia · social withdrawal · anhedonia · heightened pain

blocks.alt: stress response HPA axis and sympathetic effects - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The stress response: corticotropin-releasing factor, adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol, and catecholamines, with their effects on behaviour and the body

blocks.html: 3. Diagnosis

• Under-diagnosed and under-treated because of four myths:
    • "anyone sick will be depressed" - still a minority, and depressed patients do worse and have far higher suicide rates
    • "depression in the sick is untreatable" · "the sick can't tolerate antidepressants" - trials show efficacy and tolerability
    • "you can't tell depression from the illness" - DSM criteria still work if you weigh psychological symptoms over neurovegetative ones · screening tools are validated (Beck, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire)
  • Screen everyone: "Do you feel depressed?"
  • Red-flag symptoms - not normal in medical illness: hopelessness · worthlessness · guilt · anhedonia · suicidal ideation
  • Risk factors: family or personal psychiatric history · poorly controlled pain · more comorbidity and functional impairment
  • Inclusive approach, low threshold · when in doubt, consultation-liaison psychiatry (psychiatric care for medical inpatients)

rows: "Situational depression" - excessive reaction to an identifiable stressor, within 3 months
Persistent low mood and/or anhedonia, vegetative symptoms, possible suicidality
Acute confusion with global inattention, slowed, lethargic
Supportive psychotherapy - responds poorly to medication

blocks.html: 4. Treatment principles

• "Under-treated depression is untreated depression": start low and go slow, but reach a therapeutic dose - stop only for intolerable side effects
  • Multidisciplinary, coordinate between specialists, include caregivers
  • Options (adapt, ask if unsure): antidepressants · psychotherapy · electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) · transcranial magnetic stimulation · psychiatric admission
  • Follow-up is paramount - side effects drive non-adherence
5. Cardiac disease

• Prevalence: cardiovascular disease ~15% · bypass surgery 20% · unstable angina 15% · catheterization 17-23% · post-myocardial infarction 15-23% · heart failure 14-20%
  • Depression predicts mortality after myocardial infarction and in heart failure, and is an independent risk factor for coronary artery disease (relative risk 1.5-2, similar to smoking)
  • Shared mechanisms: ↑ platelet reactivity · ↓ heart rate variability · ↑ inflammation (C-reactive protein) · HPA hyperactivity · immune activation · norepinephrine dysregulation

rows: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) - sertraline safe and effective after myocardial infarction or unstable angina (SADHART trial) · may normalize platelets and heart rate variability

blocks.html: • Educate on treating to remission · watch drug interactions · psychotherapy and ECT as indicated
6. Diabetes

• Bidirectional: diabetes → 3× risk of depression · high-risk depressed patients → ~2.5× risk of diabetes
  • Disability is additive: diabetes 2.42 · depression 3.0 · both 7.15 (upper-year notes)
  • Shared: HPA changes · inflammation · abnormal glucose metabolism
  • Treatment: SSRIs or SNRIs first line (safe, effective) · tricyclics help neuropathic pain but worsen glycaemic control · other options may add weight and insulin resistance
  • Remission is sustained in only ~10% over 5 years → lifelong follow-up · treating depression improves glycaemic control, pain and HbA1c

lectures.name: Mood Disorders and Reproductive Life Stages
lectures.title: Mood disorders and reproductive life stages
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Blues are common, mild and gone within weeks; peripartum depression starts in pregnancy or within 4 weeks of delivery; postpartum psychosis is a rapid-onset emergency whose strongest risk factor is bipolar disorder. PMDD needs 5 symptoms, at least one mood symptom, in the luteal phase, confirmed over 2 cycles - SSRIs or drospirenone pills; the progestin-only pill fails. Valproate and carbamazepine are avoided in pregnancy; lamotrigine is safe in pregnancy but contraindicated in breastfeeding. Sertraline is preferred when breastfeeding. Perimenopausal depression risk is 2-5× higher, driven by the transition, not age.

Female vulnerability to mood disorders rises and falls with the reproductive hormones - puberty, the luteal phase, pregnancy and the postpartum, and perimenopause are each a window of risk. For each window: what it looks like, how to tell it from its look-alikes, and how to treat it safely for mother and baby.
1. Puberty: why depression is twice as common in females

• Lifetime major depression 2× higher in females across countries · the gap opens at puberty (pubertal stage, not age) and lasts through the reproductive years · equal in childhood, slightly higher in men in later life
  • Explanations, likely combined:
    • research artifact (women report more) - but the childhood and late-life ratios argue against it
    • psychosocial: inequality, discrimination, objectification, victimization · women internalize, men externalize
    • biological: estrogen and progesterone · episodes cluster at times of greatest hormone fluctuation · ↑ testosterone at puberty
  • Risk factors around menarche: stressful events, abuse, violence, poor body image · family psychiatric history, prior anxiety, pubertal timing, illness · poor family relationships, low support, poor school connection
2. Menstruation: PMS vs PMDD
• Both: symptoms in the luteal phase, resolving within a few days of menses

rows: 1-2% in the lecture note, 3-8% in the PMDD note (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.html:
• PMDD criteria: 5 or more symptoms in the week before menses in most cycles, improving within days of onset and minimal the week after · at least 1 mood symptom (lability, irritability or anger, depressed mood or hopelessness, anxiety) · confirmed by prospective daily ratings over 2 cycles · not just a flare of another disorder
  • Treatment: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) - continuous or luteal-phase only · drospirenone combined oral contraceptives (clot risk; progestin-only pill does not work) · cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT); dialectical behaviour therapy for suicidal behaviour · second line: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues with hormone add-back · refractory: hysterectomy with both ovaries removed
3. Pregnancy and the postpartum
• Estrogen and progesterone affect monoamine metabolism and serotonin receptors · stressors pile up from pregnancy to 1 year postpartum

rows: Pregnancy or within 4 weeks of delivery (~half before delivery)
Depressive episode: crying, poor bonding, guilt as a mother, anxiety, egosyntonic thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby
Confusion, disorganization, delusions about the baby, hallucinations · manic ~35%, depressive ~40%
Past depression (especially peripartum), PMDD, family history, partner violence, poor support
Bipolar disorder - the strongest (20-30% of women with it) · first pregnancy · prior episode
Psychotherapy (supportive, CBT, interpersonal therapy (IPT)) · SSRIs first line - sertraline preferred in breastfeeding, avoid paroxetine · electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) relatively safe
Psychiatric emergency - admit · benzodiazepine → antipsychotic → lithium (0.8-1.2 mmol/L) · lithium 9 months · prophylaxis next pregnancy

blocks.html:
• Neonatal adaptation syndrome after in-utero SSRIs (~30%, 3-5 days) - tapering before delivery does not prevent it but raises the risk of depression
  • Screen: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (10 items, under 5 minutes) · "can you sleep when the baby sleeps? are you eating? any scary thoughts about you or the baby?"
  • Untreated depression harms both: mother - poor self-care, substance use, preeclampsia, suicide (20% of maternal deaths in the first postpartum year) · infant - preterm birth, low birth weight, smaller head, lower Apgar, behavioural, language and attachment problems
4. Bipolar disorder in pregnancy and breastfeeding

• Relapse 70-85% without maintenance, 24-30% even with it · abrupt stopping (under 2 weeks) → 50-70% relapse
  • Pre-conception counselling for every woman of childbearing age with bipolar disorder
  • Clues: can't keep to bed rest · risk-taking · preoccupied with non-baby activities · postpartum depression preceded by agitation

rows: Avoid - up to 11% major defects · neural tube defects 5-6%, craniofacial, cleft lip or palate, limb, microcephaly
Avoid - up to 6% major defects, fewer neural tube defects than valproate

blocks.html:
• Rules: monotherapy at the lowest dose · folic acid, up to 4 mg a day on valproate or carbamazepine · options: switch to a lower-risk drug before conception, continue with known risks, or taper (e.g. through the first 12 weeks)
  • Screen: alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasound at 16-20 weeks (neural tube, heart) · fetal echocardiogram after first-trimester lithium · mania in pregnancy: ECT is relatively safe
  • After birth: close monitoring · protect sleep (scheduled feeds, support)
5. Perimenopause

• Perimenopause = the run-up to menopause plus its first year · the transition can take up to 10 years · diagnosis is retrospective · mood symptoms can precede physical ones by up to 5 years
  • Depression risk 2-5× higher in perimenopause than late menopause, falling 2-4 years after the final period → the transition, not age, is the cause · female:male ratio rises to 3-4:1
  • Theories: ① estrogen withdrawal (estrogen boosts serotonin · surgical menopause → more depression · but mood does not track measured levels) · ② domino (hot flushes and night sweats → poor sleep → depression · but prevalence is independent of physical symptoms)
  • Risk factors: ruminative, pessimistic personality · negative views of ageing · stressors, childhood adversity · smoking, inactivity, poor sleep · illness · ↑ sensitivity to estradiol swings · shorter reproductive span · unmarried, less education, financial hardship
  • Presents as major depression plus sleep disturbance, irritability, paranoid thinking, low self-esteem, poor memory and concentration, anxiety, weight gain, ↓ libido, aches
  • Differential: pre-existing depression · bipolar disorder · adjustment, bereavement · thyroid disease, primary ovarian insufficiency, iron deficiency anemia
  • Treatment: standard antidepressants (SSRIs, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclics) · CBT, IPT · short-term hormone replacement therapy to augment · exercise, sleep

lectures.name: In-Class - Mood Disorders
lectures.title: In-class: mood disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Never an antidepressant in bipolar disorder - use quetiapine, cariprazine or lurasidone for bipolar depression. Bupropion: no serotonin, so no sexual dysfunction and good for smoking. Mirtazapine: appetite and weight gain. Fluoxetine: longest half-life, least weight gain. Aripiprazole or brexpiprazole are the first-line add-ons in major depression.

A case session pulling the week together: which antidepressant for which patient, what is first line in major depression, and why bipolar depression is treated differently. Criteria and full treatment are in 05 - Depressive Disorders, 06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants and 09 - Bipolar Disorders.
1. Antidepressants to know

rows: Least weight gain · longest half-life (forgiving of missed doses)
Must know · SNRIs stronger than SSRIs - try one if an SSRI fails
Weight gain, appetite - useful in cancer with depression
No serotonin → smoking cessation, little weight gain, little sexual dysfunction
Rarely used, more side effects · MAOIs: avoid tyramine (aged cheese), best for atypical depression

blocks.html:
• SSRI sexual dysfunction is loss of desire (serotonin) - sildenafil won't fix it → switch to bupropion
  • quetiapine changes target with dose: ~25-50 mg sleep (histamine) · 150-300 mg depression · 600 mg or more psychosis (dopamine)
  • lamotrigine → remember Stevens-Johnson syndrome
2. First line in major depression

• Lifestyle: supervised exercise · light therapy
  • Psychotherapy: cognitive behavioural therapy · interpersonal therapy · behavioral activation
  • Medication: SSRIs · SNRIs · norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitors · noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants
  • Adjunct: second-generation antipsychotics aripiprazole or brexpiprazole (dopamine and serotonin) - not first-generation (dopamine only)
  • Episode symptoms: SIGECAPS (depression) · DIGFAST (mania)
3. Bipolar depression is different

• No antidepressants in bipolar disorder - they can induce mania
  • The session names 3 approved drugs for bipolar depression: quetiapine, cariprazine, lurasidone - the guideline figure in 09 - Bipolar Disorders also lists lithium and lamotrigine first line (sources differ - check the slides)
